text: A SOC's mission from Lesson 1 only holds up if the monitoring behind it never actually stops. Security incidents don't wait for business hours, which means the team watching for them can't either. This lesson covers the three real models SOCs use to actually staff that around-the-clock coverage: follow-the-sun, rotating shifts, and on-call escalation.

Automated attacks like scanning and credential-stuffing bots run continuously with no regard for the target's time zone. Ransomware crews specifically favor deploying at night, on weekends, and over holidays, betting that fewer defenders are watching and that any response will be slower. A SOC that only operates nine to five isn't watching during exactly the hours an attacker is most likely to choose on purpose.

Large, multinational organizations often solve this with follow-the-sun coverage: SOCs in the Americas, EMEA, and APAC each staff their own normal daytime hours, handing the queue to the next region as their day ends, with structured notes at each handoff. The result is continuous 24-hour coverage without any single office ever staffing an overnight shift at all.

A single-location SOC covers the same 24 hours with a rotating shift schedule instead — analysts cycle through day, evening, and overnight shifts on a set rotation, often three 8-hour shifts, so the burden of nights doesn't fall permanently on one person. Smaller teams that can't fully staff overnight back that up with on-call escalation, paging a Tier 2 or Tier 3 analyst when something exceeds what the smaller night team can handle alone.

None of these models is automatically the right one — a global enterprise, a mid-size company with one office, and a small team with a skeleton overnight crew each reach for a different combination to get the same result: real coverage with no gap. Up next, Lesson 4 looks at how a SOC actually matures over time, from purely reactive to genuinely proactive.
